Jousi- ja nuoliviini, yhdistetty. Molemmat on valmistettu parkitsemattomasta punertavalla värillä värjätystä hylkeennahasta, josta karvat on poistettu. Jousiviini on herneenpalon muotoinen pussi, joka on saatu ompelemalla yhteen kaksi nahkakaitaletta. Sisäpuolelle on leikattu suorakulmainen aukko. Jousiviinen ulompi nahkakaitale jatkuu keskellä lyhyenä läppänä, johon nuoliviini on kiinnitetty tikkauksin. Nuoliviini on tehty taittamalla nahkapala ja ompelemalla pitkä puoli kiinni. Nuoliviinen alapää on suljettu ompelemalla siihen pieni nahkapala. Yläpää on jätetty avoimeksi, mutta sen suojana on erillinen nahkainen huppu, joka on kiinnitetty viineen nahkanauhalla. Jousessa on ollut kantohihna, nyt jäljellä on vain sen kiinnitysreiät viinet yhdistävässä nahkaläpässä.





Inughuit bow case with quiver (combined). The bow case and the quiver are made of dehaired untanned sealskin painted with reddish color. The bow case is a peapod-shaped bag of two skin pieces stitched together. A rectangular opening is cut into the middle of the inner side of the case. The short piece of the case’s outer skin extends in the middle as flap and the arrow quiver is stitched to it. The quiver is a piece of skin folded on itself and stitched along the long side. A small piece of skin is sewn to close the quiver’s lower part. The open upper part is provided with a separate hood attached to the quiver with a skin thong. The bow case would have been folded when carried from a strap, now only four holes remain in the skin piece attaching the quiver to the case.

This bow case with quiver was collected in 1892 by Robert E. Peary from the Polar Inuit in Greenland for the World’s Columbian Exposition held in Chicago in 1893. After the World’s Fair most of Peary’s collection went to the Field Museum, but a few were taken by the Peabody Harvard Museum. This bow case was catalogued under number 49702 at the Peabody Harvard Museum in 1893 and held a bow and 14 arrows. In an exchange with the National Museum of Finland in 1951, the bow case was sent to Finland with another bow (n:o 49701) and 12 of the original 14 arrows in it. The bow case and arrows were collected from “the Kayamute, the Natives of Narkrassome” according to the Peabody ledger entry of 1893 – the settlement is most likely Niaqornaarsuk, which was quite close to Peary’s camp on Cape York.
